items.title: [rucio] Rucio: Unauthenticated administrator impersonation through SSH challenge tokens
items.summary: SummarySSH challenge tokens are mistakenly accepted as valid credentials during the authentication token validation process.While an SSH challenge token is intended as a short-lived nonce for use in a subsequent SSH key exchange, the function to validate authentication tokens does not differentiate between these and actual authentication tokens. Because challenge tokens are generated based on an account name provided via headers without requiring prior authentication, an unauthenticated attacker can request a valid "challenge" token for any account (including administrative ones) and use it to authenticate against other API endpoints.Proof of ConceptThe vulnerability exists because SSH challenge tokens are stored in the same database table as regular authentication tokens and validate_auth_token in lib/rucio/core/authentication.py accepts these "challenge" tokens. An attacker can obtain a challenge token for an account such as “root” via the REST API and then present it as a valid authentication bearer token:Request a challenge token for an arbitrary account (e.g., "root"):curl -i -H "X-Rucio-Account: root" https://rucio/auth/ssh_challenge_tokenThe server returns a 200 OK with the header X-Rucio-SSH-Challenge-Token.The attacker can then use this specific token within the ten-second challenge lifetime as an authentication credential in subsequent requests to the Rucio API:  curl -H "X-Rucio-Auth-Token: $CHALLENGE_TOKEN"  https://rucio/accounts/whoamiReferenceshttps://github.com/rucio/rucio/security/advisories/GHSA-x585-4vv8-2mh2https://github.com/rucio/rucio/commit/4d4a58571ba853f3a55aef16ad9eb0944fce7483https://github.com/rucio/rucio/commit/4df924feb539ef789b3e78cbc00712ef8cdf606ehttps://github.com/rucio/rucio/commit/8295d72a9e2d76abf9e98eb6f9a4ed5cb3bb1869https://github.com/rucio/rucio/commit/883d526c2f3c315cd775fb142038007053e3882bhttps://github.com/rucio/rucio/commit/b1725ee5477b683202174f0ec77ae00921bc3bd0https://github.com/rucio/rucio/commit/d7a3c2c2f933dce8edbcad07d8d076b9b782da35https://github.com/rucio/rucio/commit/e6525523e3bbe8ae34cbfc9b043ae52bda209b87https://github.com/rucio/rucio/commit/f5db3546d9c0de4642dc9aa52e6a6e447911d680https://github.com/rucio/rucio/releases/tag/35.9.1https://github.com/rucio/rucio/releases/tag/35.9.1.post1https://github.com/rucio/rucio/releases/tag/38.6.1https://github.com/rucio/rucio/releases/tag/38.6.2https://github.com/rucio/rucio/releases/tag/40.4.2https://github.com/rucio/rucio/releases/tag/41.1.1https://github.com/rucio/rucio/releases/tag/41.2.0https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-x585-4vv8-2mh2

items.title: [soupsieve] Soup Sieve: Polynomial-time denial of service in the descendant combinator
items.summary: SummaryMatching a selector that uses the descendant combinator (a b) takes time that grows polynomially with how deeply the document is nested, and each extra descendant combinator in the selector raises the degree by one. A selector with k descendant combinators takes O(n^(k+1)) time on a chain of n nested elements.An attacker who controls the HTML or XML that an application passes to Soup Sieve (directly, or through Beautiful Soup's select(), select_one(), css.select(), etc.) can send a very small, deeply nested document that keeps a CPU busy for seconds to minutes against an ordinary selector such as section div div.DetailsTo match a b, Soup Sieve checks each element against b and then walks up through its ancestors looking for one that matches a. When the selector has more descendant combinators, the rest of the selector is tried again from each ancestor on that walk, and so on for every combinator. Nothing was reused between walks, so the same ancestors were matched against the same part of the selector over and over.The worst case is when the leftmost part of the selector never matches, as in section div div against a document of nested <div> with no <section>: every walk goes all the way to the root and no search can stop early.TimingsExample timings with html.parser on Soup Sieve 3.0.4 and 4.0, using a document of nested <div> (5 bytes each) and no matches:Nesting depthInput sizeSelector3.0.44.02,00010 KBsection div1.6 s0.05 s4,00020 KBsection div5.1 s0.01 s4002 KBsection div div6.7 s< 0.01 s8004 KBsection div div53.0 s< 0.01 s1000.5 KBsection div div div2.5 s< 0.01 s2001 KBsection div div div40.9 s< 0.01 sNone of these selectors use unusual syntax.Proof of conceptimport timeimport bs4import soupsieve as svsoup = bs4.BeautifulSoup('<div>' * 200, 'html.parser')t = time.process_time()sv.select('section div div div', soup)print(time.process_time() - t)On affected versions, doubling the nesting depth multiplies the time by about 2^(k+1), where k is the number of descendant combinators: about 4x for section div, 8x for section div div, and 16x for section div div div.ImpactApplications are affected if they run selectors with descendant combinators against documents that untrusted users can influence, such as scrapers, HTML sanitizers or filters, and services that process uploaded or fetched markup. Descendant combinators are among the most common parts of CSS selectors, and a document of about 1 KB is enough to tie up a worker for close to a minute. Applications that only run selectors against trusted documents are not affected.PatchesFixed in 4.0 by facelessuser/soupsieve#351. Whether an element is, or has an ancestor that is, a match for part of a selector depends only on its parent, so Soup Sieve now caches that result per element and relation for every element visited on the walk. Each descendant combinator is then linear in the size of the document. Results are unchanged, and ordinary documents are no slower.Caching is enabled by default, so no changes are needed beyond upgrading. The NOCACHE flag is a temporary fallback for users who run into problems with caching, and it is planned for removal. It uses the old uncached matching, so selectors compiled with NOCACHE are still subject to polynomial time and shouldn't be used with descendant combinators on untrusted input.WorkaroundsIf users can't upgrade:Use as few descendant combinators as they can in selectors that run on untrusted documents. Where the structure of thedocument is known, the child combinator (a > b) only looks at the parent and is not affected.Limit the size and nesting depth of untrusted documents before selecting on them.Run selection on untrusted input with a time limit, for example in a worker process that can be stopped.Referenceshttps://github.com/facelessuser/soupsieve/security/advisories/GHSA-mmhr-3c5m-f64fhttps://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-126190https://github.com/facelessuser/soupsieve/pull/351https://github.com/facelessuser/soupsieve/commit/ff1a5ce7e5addc31626d7b6053511fecdb4f6320https://github.com/facelessuser/soupsieve/releases/tag/4.0https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mmhr-3c5m-f64f

items.title: [soupsieve] Soup Sieve: General sibling combinator inside :has() matches untrusted HTML in quadratic time
items.summary:
SummaryMatching a selector that puts a general-sibling combinator inside :has(), such as div:has(a ~ b), against untrusted HTML runs in O(n²) time in the number of sibling elements. A single small document with a few thousand siblings ties the process up for a minute of CPU, so an application that runs a fixed selector of this shape over HTML it doesn't control can be stalled by one request.:has is powerful, but much in the same way poor regular expressions can be crafted to cause catastrophic backtracking with greedy capturing, has can be used to create non-ideal scenarios that can cause large portions of the tree to be evaluated for one or many elements if not used thoughtfully.This behavior is not exclusive to Soup Sieve, but browsers make note of these potential performance issues themselves: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Reference/Selectors/:has#performance_considerations.With all of that said, there is room for improvements that can in some cases greatly improve performance.Details:has(a ~ b) asks "does this element contain an a that has a later sibling b?". When no b is present, soupsieve can't short-circuit, and it answers the question with a nested scan: match_future_child walks every candidate a under the scope, and for each one the general-sibling branch of match_future_relations walks all of that a's following siblings looking for b. With n siblings that is (n-1) + (n-2) + ... + 1 comparisons, i.e. O(n²).The adjacent-sibling form div:has(a + b) stays linear, because its branch checks only the one immediately following sibling per candidate. So the cost is specific to the general-sibling ~ (and ~ nested inside :has), and it shows up on the common case where the right-hand side simply isn't there.Proof of conceptInstalled from PyPI: pip install soupsieve==2.9.2 beautifulsoup4.import timeimport soupsievefrom bs4 import BeautifulSoupselector = "div:has(a ~ b)"for n in (1000, 2000, 4000, 8000): html = "
" + ("" * n) + "
" soup = BeautifulSoup(html, "html.parser") start = time.perf_counter() soupsieve.select(selector, soup) print(n, round((time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000), "ms")Measured:n=1000 837 msn=2000 3667 msn=4000 14797 msn=8000 59746 msTime quadruples for each doubling of n. The n=8000 input is a ~56 KB HTML fragment.ImpactAvailability. Any caller that evaluates a fixed selector containing a general sibling under :has() over attacker-controlled markup can be forced to spend minutes of CPU on a small input. The selector is developer-authored and ordinary; the untrusted part is the HTML, which is soupsieve's normal input.A single-pass evaluation of the sibling run (remember whether an a has been seen while scanning the siblings once) would make this case linear.MitigationQuadratic time for :has in some circumstances is expected and not a bug. While we've made optimizations and there may be more in the future, the way :has is designed to operate will never perform in linear time in all circumstances. Users should thoughtfully apply the use of :has.The anchor selector (the A in A:has(B)) should not be an element that has too many children. Additionally, too general an anchor, such as *, can cause :has() to be applied to every element.Further, it is recommended that the inner selector (the B in A:has(B)) should use combinators like > or + to limit traversal. When the selector inside :has() is not tightly constrained, Soup Sieve might need to traverse the entire subtree of the anchorelement to check the condition.If the risk for a given project is too great, user input can be scanned for usage of :has and be denied. Calls can also be wrapped in a timeout to prevent long-running processes as well.Referenceshttps://github.com/facelessuser/soupsieve/security/advisories/GHSA-4j63-6c4x-wfg4https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-126192https://github.com/facelessuser/soupsieve/pull/304https://github.com/facelessuser/soupsieve/commit/ffb88cca745c591224f74a8e86414a85e8f35fc0https://github.com/facelessuser/soupsieve/releases/tag/2.10https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4j63-6c4x-wfg4

items.title: [Pillow] Pillow: Memory DoS in TIFF and EXIF IFD parsing via overlapping tag data
items.summary: ============================================================================ANT-2026-D7STJUWL  [medium]  CWE-770  dosMemory DoS in TIFF and EXIF IFD parsing via overlapping tag dataLocation: src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:927  in ImageFileDirectory_v2.load()Commit:   a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6============================================================================A small, crafted image file can make Pillow use thousands of times its own size in memory while the file is only being opened, which lets anyone who can submit an image crash or stall the process handling it. A 144 KB TIFF makes Image.open() return normally while holding 1.6 GiB of memory. The largest such standard TIFF, about 786 KB, asks for roughly 48 GiB, which in practice gets the worker killed by the operating system. The file declares a 1×1 image, so the decompression-bomb check never triggers and no warning is raised. There is no memory corruption; the impact is denial of service.The bug is in ImageFileDirectory_v2.load() in src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py (around line 927). For every directory entry whose value is stored elsewhere in the file, it reads that value into a new bytes object with ImageFile._safe_read(fp, count * unit_size) and keeps it in _tagdata. _safe_read() only checks that the bytes exist. Nothing limits the total read across entries, and nothing stops every entry from pointing at the same bytes. An attacker can therefore give each of N distinct private tags an offset and count that covers the whole file, at a cost of 12 bytes per entry. Memory grows as N × file size, which is quadratic in the file size, and BigTIFF removes the 65,535-entry ceiling.The same loop parses EXIF data, so the problem reaches beyond TIFF:A 66 KB JPEG APP1 segment costs about 340 MiB inside Image.open() itself, via _read_dpi_from_exif().A 96 KB PNG eXIf chunk costs 754 MiB on getexif() or ImageOps.exif_transpose().WebP EXIF and MPO reach the same code.The attached reproducer builds a 72 KB TIFF and a 72 KB PNG. Using only Image.open() and getexif(), each causes 412 MiB of tag data to be retained, about 6,000 times the file size. The loop dates to the original PIL 1.1.7 import, so every Pillow release since 1.0 is affected.DetailsTiffImagePlugin.ImageFileDirectory_v2.load() reads the out-of-line value of every IFD entry into its own bytes object and keeps it in self._tagdata. Nothing bounds the sum of those reads, and nothing prevents every entry from pointing at the same region of the file. An IFD with N entries whose (offset, count) each cover the whole file therefore costs N × filesize bytes of memory, while the IFD itself costs only 12 bytes per entry. This one loop is the IFD parser for TIFF frames and for Image.Exif alike, so it is reachable from Image.open() on a TIFF or JPEG and from getexif() / ImageOps.exif_transpose() on PNG, JPEG, WebP and MPO.Observed on the stock build at this commit: a valid 144,110-byte 1×1 greyscale TIFF with 12,000 such entries makes Image.open() return normally (no exception, no warning, 1 declared pixel so MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS is irrelevant) after 1.5 s, with the process RSS grown from 15 MiB to 1,671 MiB and im.tag_v2 holding 1,649 MiB of tag data for as long as the image object lives. The same IFD placed in the eXIf chunk of a 96 KB PNG makes im.getexif() retain 754 MiB. A 65,870-byte JPEG whose APP1 Exif segment is such an IFD (5,400 entries × 65,519 bytes) allocates ~340 MiB inside Image.open() itself, with no further call.# src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:902-946  (ImageFileDirectory_v2.load)for i in range(tag_count):    tag, typ, count, data = ( … self._unpack("HHL4s", self._ensure_read(fp, 12)))    …    size = count * unit_size                         # 918: attacker-chosen    if size > (8 if self._bigtiff else 4):        here = fp.tell()        (offset,) = self._unpack("Q" if self._bigtiff else "L", data)        …        fp.seek(offset)                              # 926: attacker-chosen        data = ImageFile._safe_read(fp, size)        # 927: new bytes object of `size`        fp.seek(here)    …    self._tagdata[tag] = data                        # 945: kept    self.tagtype[tag] = typImageFile._safe_read() only guarantees that size bytes are actually present in the stream (it reads in SAFEBLOCK chunks and raises on truncation); it is a guard against allocating for data that does not exist, not against reading the same existing data many times. For a well-formed file each entry points at its own disjoint value, so the total read is at most the file size. For the crafted file every one of the N entries has a distinct tag number (so none overwrites another in _tagdata), type BYTE, count = filesize - 1 and offset = 1; each iteration allocates and fills a fresh filesize - 1-byte object and stores it. load() does not care whether the tag number is known or whether the type makes sense for it; any 16-bit tag number and any type in _load_dispatch is accepted. Memory is N × filesize, and since filesize ≈ 12 N,

items.title: [Pillow] Pillow: Heap buffer overflow saving TIFF with libtiff when tags override image size
items.summary: ============================================================================ANT-2026-CS7N494P  [high]  CWE-787  memory-safetyHeap buffer overflow saving TIFF with libtiff when tags override image sizeLocation: src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:1035  in ImagingLibTiffEncode()Commit:   a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6============================================================================When Pillow saves an image as a compressed TIFF, size information taken from the image's metadata can make the encoder read past the end of a heap buffer. Someone who uploads an image can use this to get the server process's memory, including pointers, copied into the saved file, or to crash the process. When the metadata also enables TIFF "Predictor=2" compression, the encoder writes past the buffer instead, corrupting the heap and aborting the process. This affects applications that write TIFF through libtiff (any compression= other than raw) and either carry the source metadata across with exif=im.getexif() / tiffinfo=, or simply re-save a crafted palette TIFF with Image.open(f).save(out, "TIFF"), which inherits its compression and predictor from the upload.In TiffImagePlugin._save's libtiff branch, only BitsPerSample is pinned to the real image when the tag list for the encoder is built (src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:1955). ImageWidth, ImageLength and PlanarConfiguration are set from im.size but are then overwritten by the exif=/tiffinfo= merge loop at :1768-1772. SamplesPerPixel is never set for single-band modes, so a value from the caller's tags or from the source TIFF's own IFD reaches TIFFSetField. ImagingLibTiffEncode then passes a row buffer sized from the actual image (src/encode.c:291) to TIFFWriteScanline (src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:1035) with no check against TIFFScanlineSize(), and libtiff consumes a full scanline of the tag-described width from it.The attached reproducer demonstrates the read case. A 64x4 greyscale JPEG whose EXIF says SamplesPerPixel=3, Photometric=RGB is converted into a valid RGB TIFF in which 128 bytes of each row are live heap, including pointers that change from run to run. The same JPEG with EXIF ImageWidth=2**27 kills the process with SIGSEGV. For the write case, the values written are byte-wise differences of existing heap contents rather than attacker-chosen data, and nothing beyond the observed glibc abort is shown. The tiffinfo= route dates back to Pillow 2.3.0 (dbf47837ce99), and the exif= route to 8.4.0 (c0f619384cbc).DetailsWhen an image is saved as TIFF through the libtiff encoder (any compression= other than raw, or TiffImagePlugin.WRITE_LIBTIFF), libtiff sizes its scanline from the ImageWidth / SamplesPerPixel / BitsPerSample / PlanarConfiguration tags it was handed, Pillow sizes the encoder row buffer from the real image, and nothing compares the two. In TiffImagePlugin._save's libtiff branch only BitsPerSample is pinned in the attribute dict given to the encoder (atts, src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:1955-1982); the other geometry tags can come from caller- or attacker-supplied data:ImageWidth (256), ImageLength (257) and PlanarConfiguration (284) are set from im.size before the tiffinfo= / exif= merge loop at :1768-1772, so they are overwritten by it — by the EXIF of an uploaded JPEG, or by stale geometry in im.getexif() / im.tag_v2 of a TIFF that Pillow auto-transposed on load (Orientation tag) or that the application thumbnail()ed.SamplesPerPixel (277) is only put in the IFD for multi-band modes (:1847-1850), so for single-band images (L, P, I;16, 1, …) a value from exif= / tiffinfo=, or from the source TIFF's own IFD via supplied_tags (im.tag_v2, :1782), is forwarded to libtiff. A palette TIFF with SamplesPerPixel=2, BitsPerSample=(8,8), ExtraSamples=(0,) opens as mode P (rawmode PX, extra sample dropped), and a bare im.save(out, "TIFF") — no save arguments; compression and Predictor are inherited from the source — already makes libtiff process 2*width bytes per row from a width-byte buffer.ImagingLibTiffEncode then hands the image-sized row buffer to TIFFWriteScanline, and libtiff reads one scanline of the tag-described geometry out of a buffer holding one row of the actual image. With Predictor = 2 (also forwarded from tiffinfo= / im.tag_v2) libtiff's horizontal differencing first rewrites the whole scanline in place, so the over-read becomes an out-of-bounds heap write on every row.The tags do not have to be supplied deliberately by the application: im.getexif() of an uploaded JPEG returns whatever IFD0 tags the file carries, and the common metadata-preserving conversionim = Image.open(uploaded_jpeg)                                   # 64x4, mode "L"im.save(out, "TIFF", exif=im.getexif(), compression="tiff_lzw")behaves as follows on the stock build at this commit:EXIF IFD0 {277: 3, 262: 2} (SamplesPerPixel=3, Photometric=RGB): the save succeeds and out is a 64x4 RGB TIFF.
